JSON: Name: super_net_uncertainty_segmentation Title: Bayesian uncertainty propagation in encoder-decoder networks for medical image segmentation Short Hypothesis: Analytically propagating the posterior mean and covariance through encoder-decoder layers using first-order Taylor approximations produces higher segmentation robustness (measured by mean Dice similarity under specified Gaussian noise and adversarial perturbations) and more accurate pixel-wise uncertainty localization than MC-dropout and ensemble baselines. Related Work: Existing approaches for uncertainty-aware segmentation fall into three classes: post-hoc sampling with MC-dropout, model ensembles, and variational approaches that estimate parameter uncertainty. MC-dropout obtains predictive uncertainty via multiple stochastic forward passes at inference and is inexpensive to train but requires repeated evaluations and often yields poorly calibrated uncertainty for pixel-level segmentation. Ensembles improve uncertainty fidelity but incur multiplicative training and storage cost and are expensive at inference. Prior variational-moments propagation work demonstrated analytic moment propagation for convolutional classifiers but did not address encoder-decoder architectures or decoder-specific operations (up-sampling, padding, concatenation) and produced low-dimensional or scalar uncertainty measures rather than dense per-pixel covariance. Current methods therefore either (a) estimate uncertainty only at inference time via sampling, (b) lack analytic propagation through decoder operations, or (c) provide coarse uncertainty summaries; none jointly learn and propagate pixel-level predictive covariance through full encoder-decoder pipelines at training time while maintaining practical inference cost. Abstract: This project addresses trustworthy medical image segmentation by learning and propagating predictive uncertainty throughout encoder-decoder networks. We propose a Bayesian framework that represents convolutional kernels as Gaussian random variables and analytically propagates their posterior first and second moments across encoder and decoder layers using first-order Taylor approximations. The method produces two simultaneous outputs at inference: a segmentation map (predictive mean) and a dense pixel-wise uncertainty map (predictive covariance) without Monte Carlo sampling. Key contributions include closed-form moment propagation rules for decoder operations (up-sampling, padding, concatenation), an ELBO-based training objective that updates mean and covariance, and demonstration of uncertainty localization under noise and adversarial perturbations. Expected outcomes are improved segmentation robustness under corrupted inputs and uncertainty maps that correlate with segmentation errors, enabling automated identification of low-confidence regions while avoiding repeated inference passes or large ensembles. Experiments: Datasets: 1) Lung CT segmentation (public chest CT collection, 2D slices, binary lung labels), 2) Hippocampus MRI (Medical Segmentation Decathlon, 2D slices, anterior/posterior labels), 3) BraTS HGG multi-modal MRI (T1,T1c,T2,FLAIR, 2D slices or 3D slices, multi-class labels), 4) UAB clinical FLAIR brain tumor dataset (2D FLAIR, expert tumor masks). Baselines: deterministic U-Net (cross-entropy), MC-dropout U-Net (dropout at central blocks, N=20 stochastic forward passes), ensemble of 5 independently trained U-Nets, and a variational-moments-propagation classifier adapted to segmentation where applicable. Metrics: per-class Dice similarity coefficient (DSC), mean DSC across test set, predictive calibration (expected calibration error, ECE), predictive entropy and average predictive variance, uncertainty–error correlation (Spearman's rho between per-pixel variance and binary error map), area under the retention curve (AURC) and Dice after removal of top-k uncertain pixels, inference latency (ms/image), and storage footprint (MB). Experimental setup: train/val/test splits ~80/10/10; identical U-Net backbone capacity across methods; SUPER-Net trained by minimizing ELBO with Gaussian variational posterior and diagonal covariance propagation; deterministic baselines trained with standard losses; Adam optimizer lr=0.001. Robustness tests: add additive Gaussian noise at SNR levels {40,30,20,10,3} dB applied either to whole image or to target regions only; generate adversarial attacks using untargeted FGSM and targeted PGD with up to 20 iterations and step size 1 (report SNR-equivalent perturbation levels). Statistical analysis: report mean±std over 5 random seeds and perform paired Wilcoxon signed-rank tests for DSC differences (alpha=0.05). Ablations: (A1) FULL vs DIAGONAL covariance propagation in SUPER-Net, (A2) propagate only mean (deterministic) vs propagate mean+covariance, (A3) first-order Taylor approximation vs second-order approximation (where tractable), (A4) vary prior variance hyperparameter sigma_prior ∈ {0.01,0.1,1.0}. Report per-ablation changes in DSC, ECE, and uncertainty–error correlation. Risk Factors and Limitations: Approximation error: first-order Taylor expansions can underestimate or misrepresent predictive covariance in strongly nonlinear regions, producing miscalibrated uncertainty. Covariance modeling: using diagonal covariance for scalability ignores inter-feature correlations and may reduce uncertainty localization fidelity. Prior and hyperparameter sensitivity: model behavior depends on chosen Gaussian priors and KL weighting; poor choices can yield overconfident or overly diffuse predictions. Computational cost: propagating mean and covariance increases per-layer computation and inference latency compared to a single deterministic forward pass; memory usage increases for per-kernel variance parameters and intermediate covariance buffers. Data limitations: class imbalance and small sample sizes (rare structures) can bias learned uncertainty and reduce generalization. Adversarial limitations: adversaries may be constructed to target uncertainty estimates (uncertainty-aware attacks) and circumvent detection. Architecture generalization: derived propagation rules may not transfer directly to non-convolutional modules (transformers, self-attention) without additional derivations. Evaluation bias: results may depend on chosen datasets, noise models, and attack parameters and may not generalize to all clinical imaging modalities or 3D volumetric pipelines.
